title: trying to add memory to a trading system without making it overfit
author: AzimuthSystems
selftext:
i'm building something called AZIMUTH. still very early, mostly research/replay/paper right now.

one thing i'm playing with is giving it a memory of past setups. basically save what the market looked like, what happened after, then compare that with new setups later.

the part i'm stuck on is how to do that without slowly teaching it noise. i don't want the logic to become "this lost once, never do it again". more like "similar situations usually did this" and use that as one input.

has anyone here tried something like this? curious what worked and what just turned into overfitting

comments.author: NefariousnessOpening
comments.body:
If you define memory as the same kinda of systems generally used with agents I don’t believe overfiitting can occur. Unless you also have ML Ops in the runtime. Noise is a common problem because the entries to the data store will be a flat pile of information with no real information about the significance of one thing vs another. Contradictions are also a high likelihood and the slowdown of the process is correlated to the size of the store in some cases. When you say setups I’m inferring that as an entry + market conditions at the time and maybe also the exit strategy, port size, etc. I have no idea if comparing now to past scenarios is helpful but I’m curious now. My immediate thought is that it would have little useful implications. If you want to gain leverage from past setups/data, I would not use memory to define it. I would lean towards ML OPs and design a Feature store, implement something like DuckDB and Parquet tables. And / or I’d be thinking about constructing a golden set. This is a good alignment with my understanding of what you described 

Especially a golden set 

Take for example 500 historical setups with known outcomes and the full set if data to reconstruct that ‘moment’ of the market. You can evaluate current setups against the golden set. I’m oversimplifying this a bit. You also need to be precise about the data engineering and careful about accuracy of point in time, prevent look ahead leakage, etc

With the golden set you could train a classifier and derive a measured baseline 

This would enable a solid core. Along with this you could then implement a calibrated scorer of some sort. The scorer could function as a gate with parameters to define uncertainty bounds. It’s a way to have decision rules and reduce the guesswork

replies.author: AzimuthSystems
replies.body: yeah this is much closer to what i had in mind. golden set + calibrated scorer makes more sense than dumping everything into agent memory. how would you handle regime drift though? keep the golden set fixed as a benchmark and retrain on a separate rolling set?

replies.author: NefariousnessOpening
replies.body:
Oh yeah well off top from memory I think the rule is you have to freeze golden set train not so much and then it’s gotta be a new one. TBH I am less able to recall the specifics because some point maybe earlier this year idk. Not that long ago I grasped the concept that fine tuning like that is not necessary for most use cases. It’s not deprecated but like the ideas coming up are next level. Like RL but not a dataset, instead folding the code base into the transformer layers.

Didn’t even mention this but there are other LLM architectures that are actually much more aligned with trading. There’s also just memory. Not what I most often hear people use memory to mean. But the memory that is either loosely modeled on human memory, so working, episodic, functional, long term, etc. which the artificial hippocampus of some sort or a dreaming function. Knowledge graph, vector store, markdown value and relational database are combined into a single memory system. Just a default design not the only one. But the idea is to make the agent more capable over time in real time without having to fine tune frequently or at all. Trade offs though. 

Drift is a great thing to bring up and it happens in multiple ways and different parts of system. Actor/critic and advisor agent patterns are decent and dropping the amount of drift in an easily accessible way. Collecting the actual output of agent runtimes, the logs,  
Trace, etc is a great use case for fine tuning. It should be possible to fine tune based on this sort of data and not have to do it again soon . I think this is more likely my opinion or understanding than fact though as far as my preference to lean more to a live data pipeline vs periodic ml ops
